### Remarks

This section illustrated the four assumptions of the **FFRCISTG**—the foundation of modern causal inference in epidemiology: **no contagion** and **no interference**, which restrict the graph; **identical structural distributions**, a statement about the structural equations and error distributions that govern the causal process as it plays out within each observational unit; and **single-world independence**, the causal assumption. Together they make the observational units independent and identically distributed.

Students of causal inference might be surprised that the identification assumptions—**exchangeability** and **consistency**—are not mentioned explicitly. That is because, within the FFRCISTG framework, these assumptions are not external requirements but direct consequences of the model itself.

**Consistency** follows from the equality of the structural functions and error terms that define counterfactual and observed outcomes within a causal model. **Exchangeability**, in turn, arises from the independence of one-step-ahead counterfactuals (assumption (4) of @def-ffrcistg) and the recursive structure of the **NPSEM**. No contagion and no interference together are the no-interference part of the stable unit treatment value assumption (SUTVA).

In the next section, we relax the assumption of no interference, introduce **homogeneity** assumptions about the process of interference, and arrive at a model called the **Network FFRCISTG**, which allows us to reason about causality in the presence of a fixed pattern of interference.
